dossiers.catalyst_stack: On 26 Apr 2026 Noble added about $565 million of backlog, including a Petrobras extension of Noble Courage through December 2030 and a Woodside award for Noble Deliverer, then booked about $200 million more on 27 Jul and a Tullow Ghana campaign for Faye Kozack on 28 Sep. The 27 Jul Q2 print flipped the year: $720 million of revenue, a $37 million net loss, $43 million of Brazil idle time on Faye Kozack and Courage, and a cut in FY2026 revenue and adjusted EBITDA guidance. Street followed, with Citi and Susquehanna cutting targets in late June and early July, Barclays staying Overweight but trimming its PT after the miss, and the stock dropping 9.07% to $39.20 on 28 Jul. Cleanup was mixed—an 11 Jun refinancing into 6.250% 2034 notes versus a $42 million Ocean Apex scrap impairment—while the 30 Sep geo/oil bounce is sector beta, not a company-specific inflection.
dossiers.key_assumption: Brazil suspensions and the 2026 guide-down are a utilization air pocket rather than lost franchise, so 2027–30 contracts (Courage, Tullow, Viking, Deliverer) hold without a second guidance cut or a break in the $2.00 dividend.

dossiers.catalyst_stack: Transocean added more than $2 billion of floater backlog between April 2 and August 20, capped by the June 30 Equinor seven-rig-year package worth over $1 billion at a $399,000 base day rate plus ONGC’s $300 million KG2 award. On August 5 the company reported Q2 non-GAAP EPS of $0.03 and $966 million of contract-drilling revenue, both beats, and raised full-year 2026 revenue guidance to $3,900–$3,975 million, prompting Fearnley’s August 7 upgrade to Buy. CFIUS approved the Valaris combination on June 29, but the May 4 DOJ Second Request still extends HSR review and remains the principal negative binary. The September 24 SDNY dismissal of the securities class action, a 30% short float, and continued fixture flow leave the near-term setup skewed to the upside if antitrust clearance holds.
dossiers.key_assumption: Valaris receives DOJ/HSR clearance and Equinor’s license-conditional seven-rig-year agreement plus 2026–27 fixtures convert at stated backlog without an oil-driven offshore capex freeze.

dossiers.catalyst_stack: On July 23, 2026, SkyWest raised its buyback authorization by $250 million and agreed to purchase and operate 11 new E175s for American Airlines, even after April 23 guidance eased full-year GAAP EPS to about $11 on fuel and slightly lower summer block hours. Goldman Sachs cut the stock to Neutral and a $108 target on July 2 citing weaker partner-driven block-hour growth, while TD Cowen later lifted its Buy target to $123 on August 24 after earlier Citi and Cowen hikes. Governance and signaling turned mixed in July: the Fifth Circuit on July 9 affirmed an EEOC Title VII judgment with punitive damages, Wade Steel became airline President and COO the same day, and CEO Chip Childs and CFO Robert Simmons sold 50,500 and 25,000 shares on July 28–29. Sioux City’s council on September 28 recommended a four-year EAS award for SkyWest from January 2027, and airline shares caught a bid on September 30 as oil prices dropped.
dossiers.key_assumption: Most jet-fuel cost remains CPA-reimbursed, the American E175s and Sioux City EAS recommendation convert into flown block hours, and July officer sales plus Goldman’s growth cut do not foreshadow a 2027 utilization or rate reset.

dossiers.catalyst_stack: On June 15, 2026 the board added a $500 million buyback and reinstated a $0.03 quarterly dividend, then closed the Çöpler sale on June 24 for about $1.49 billion cash and finished the Hod Maden exit on July 17 via an uncapped 4% NSR. Growth capex was raised on September 28 at Marigold, CC&V, Seabee and Puna without changing production guidance, while the Phenom/Dobbin Nevada option (June 29–September 30) is a small bolt-on around a cash-rich Americas portfolio.
dossiers.key_assumption: Gold prices and H2-weighted 2026 mine delivery hold, so the Turkey-exit cash, buyback, and U.S. case dismissal keep the re-rating without an AISC/guidance cut or a heap-leach/Puna shock.
